OpenAI faces two core challenges: first, try to avoid network congestion as much as possible—while some bottlenecks cannot be eliminated (such as two GPUs sending data to the same destination at the same time), congestion in other cases can be avoided through design; second, minimize the impact of network failures on training jobs—at a sufficiently large scale, even the highest-quality network will experience continuous link and switch failures. In the past, a single failure could crash the training job, either restarting from the last checkpoint or waiting for the network to recompute routes, a process that could take tens of seconds—a huge waste of GPU compute and time. In synchronous pretraining scenarios, where thousands of GPUs collaborate across machines and train the same model in lockstep, the impact of any single link glitch is magnified many times over.

Traditional AI training network protocols require each transmission to take a fixed path to ensure packets arrive in order. In large multi-plane networks, this creates two problems: different flows colliding on the same link causing congestion, and each flow can only use one plane. 1r934ny:160: For link failures between GPU network interfaces and Tier-0 switches, training used to fail as soon as a link dropped. The faulty link usually recovers within a minute, and MRC immediately puts the plane back into use. In practice, the performance degradation caused by a lost interface link is often much smaller than the proportional physical bandwidth loss.

This reduces misjudgment and avoids mistaking congestion loss for path failure.
